item.title: One Identity Unveils Active Roles 8.6 with Enhanced Security and Administration
item.description:
Active Roles 8.6: Cumulative security, feature and administration upgrades 

One Identity has introduced Active Roles 8.6, strengthening secure and streamlined Active Directory administration with cumulative platform improvements, expanded API capabilities and greater authentication flexibility.

Active Roles 8.6, updated July 27, 2026, focuses on security and cumulative platform improvements. It fixes an RSTS configuration security issue and supersedes versions 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. Compared with Active Roles 8.2.1 SP6, One Identity says 8.6 incorporates the features, enhancements and resolved issues delivered across that intervening release line. See the Active Roles 8.6 Release Notes.

The recent improvements are therefore best described as an administrator and integration experience upgrade, rather than a new visual redesign. The cumulative release line adds capabilities including the Active Roles REST API, as well as Redistributable Secure Token Server capabilities supporting API access and SAML 2.0 federated authentication. 

Active Roles 8.6: Familiar Administration Meets Greater Flexibility and Consolidation 

Those upgrades complement one of Active Roles’ most recognizable usability strengths: a flexible, configurable UI that can be tailored to individual users and personas. Its thick-client interface is designed to resemble the familiar Microsoft Active Directory experience, helping reduce the learning curve for experienced AD administrators. 

The broader experience centers on consolidation, with a single console spanning Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 helping administrators avoid constantly switching between separate management environments. Together with PowerShell and VBScript support, the product keeps familiar tools and interaction patterns at the center of the administrator experience. 

This combination of configurable views, familiar administration and centralized control supports Active Roles’ position among top Active Directory management solutions. 

#1 Peerspot Position Strengthens the Ease-of-Administration Story 

PeerSpot currently ranks Active Roles by One Identity #1 in Active Directory Management, with an 8.5/10 rating based on 92 reviews. It also reports the largest category mindshare at 11.7%, up from 10.4% year over year, and identifies Active Roles as the category’s most popular solution by searches. [peerspot.com] 

The PeerSpot assessment highlights automated user provisioning, lifecycle management, role-based access control, password resets and streamlined account management among capabilities that reduce manual effort. 

Feature in focus: Administrator experience with Active Roles 8.6 

Active Roles 8.6 is an administrator-experience evolution, combining cumulative security, API and authentication improvements with the product’s established configurable UI, familiar Microsoft-style experience and consolidated hybrid administration.

One Identity delivers trusted identity security for enterprises worldwide to protect and simplify access to digital identities. With flexible deployment options and subscription terms – from self-managed to fully managed – our solutions integrate seamlessly into your identity fabric to strengthen your identity perimeter, protect against breaches, and ensure governance and compliance. item.title: Monetizing compliance: New AI revenue streams for regional CSPs
item.description:
The rush to adopt artificial intelligence has hit a regulatory and geopolitical wall. For governments, financial institutions, healthcare networks, and critical infrastructure operators, standard public AI models present risks. Sending sensitive data across borders or exposing proprietary data to multitenant public environments can violate compliance mandates.

This tension creates an extraordinary market opportunity for cloud service providers (CSPs). By launching sovereign AI services—environments where data, models, and execution remain strictly within national, regional, or specific legal jurisdictions—local and regional CSPs can capture a highly lucrative, rapidly expanding segment of enterprise cloud spend.

Monetizing this trend requires moving beyond standard infrastructure provisioning. It demands high-performance, legally isolated environments engineered to handle intense AI workloads without sacrificing control.

The business case for sovereign AI

Traditional public clouds thrive on global scale, but sovereign AI relies on local trust. For CSPs, building a sovereign AI offering allows them to capture revenue from organizations that previously could not use AI due to legal restrictions.

By operating a sovereign platform, CSPs can package, resell, and manage multiple value-added services:

  • Enterprise inferencing: Localized deployment of large language models (LLMs) for specific data querying.
  • Model customization: Fine-tuning base open-source models using highly classified or proprietary customer data.
  • Industry-specific AI applications: Compliant platforms customized for regional healthcare codes or localized banking laws.

CSPs can position themselves as trusted partners rather than just infrastructure vendors, commanding premium margins for compliance and isolation.

Overcoming architectural hurdles with purpose-built AI infrastructure

To successfully launch a sovereign AI business, a CSP must overcome two primary architectural challenges: raw computational efficiency and operational multitenancy. AI workloads are computationally expensive. Attempting to build an AI infrastructure on legacy cloud hardware will quickly erode margins.

To make the economics work, CSPs require full-stack technology optimized for heavy machine learning workloads. HPE and AMD provide high-performance architectures designed specifically for this use case.

By leveraging HPE AI/HPC systems powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors and AMD Instinct™ GPUs, CSPs gain access to the same technology powering the world’s fastest supercomputers delivered at their scale. In benchmarking environments, 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors deliver up to 1.73x more throughput for end-to-end AI benchmarks and 1.93x more throughput for machine learning workloads compared with competing x86 options. This massive throughput jump translates directly into lower energy costs, faster model processing times, and higher profit margins per tenant.

Real-world proof: Building sovereign supercomputers

The practicality of this architecture is highlighted by major deployments across Europe, where digital sovereignty laws are the strictest in the world.

For instance, the LUMI supercomputer located in Finland—built by HPE and powered by AMD—serves as a primary engine for European research and enterprise development. It provides an isolated, highly secure, energy-efficient ecosystem where regional organizations can train complex models without exporting data into foreign cloud frameworks.

Similarly, the Adastra supercomputer at CINES in France uses an HPE and AMD architecture to deliver world-class AI capability within a strictly governed, state-backed environment.

These massive systems demonstrate that the combined HPE-AMD platform scales efficiently. Regional CSPs can apply this architectural framework at an enterprise tier to service local banks, municipal governments, and healthcare providers.

Operating sovereign AI at scale

A successful sovereign cloud cannot just be secure; it must also be manageable. To monetize the platform effectively, CSPs need automated tools to provision resources, track consumption, and isolate individual tenants.

The HPE and AMD ecosystem solves this with software integration designed for cloud service providers:

  • Tenant isolation and control: HPE Morpheus Software provides a centralized control plane for orchestration and automation across virtual machines and containers. This allows CSPs to guarantee customers that their workloads are securely isolated from other organizations on the same system.
  • Full-stack observability: HPE OpsRamp Software gives operators deep, real-time visibility into AI infrastructure health, monitoring workloads, compute cycles, and network traffic.
  • Automated metering: Built-in resource tracking allows CSPs to easily create usage-based billing models for their enterprise clients, ensuring accurate chargebacks for compute time.

Furthermore, for highly restrictive environments, the architecture supports air-gapped management tools, allowing operations to run completely disconnected from the public internet.

Turn compliance into profit

Sovereign AI is more than an IT upgrade; it is a significant commercial differentiator. As compliance mandates tighten, businesses will migrate away from unsecured platforms toward trusted, localized cloud service providers. By building on a foundation of HPE systems with AMD processing power, CSPs can deliver supercomputing performance with regulatory compliance, unlocking brand-new, predictable revenue streams.

Ready to capture the multibillion-dollar sovereign AI opportunity?

item.title: The CIO dilemma: Scaling production AI without breaking the power grid
item.description:
The corporate mandate for CIOs has undergone a fundamental shift. It is no longer enough to simply manage IT infrastructure or treat artificial intelligence (AI) as a series of isolated experiments. Today, the focus is squarely on operationalizing high-performance computing and AI to drive measurable breakthroughs, all while navigating intense pressure regarding energy efficiency, cost management, and data center scalability.

For years, supercomputing was considered the exclusive domain of national research labs and elite academic institutions. However, the collaborative engineering between HPE and AMD has effectively bridged this gap. By migrating the architectural innovations used in the world’s most powerful supercomputers into enterprise systems, they are helping organizations solve complex real-world data challenges at scale.

Accelerating extreme workloads: Real-world impacts

When high-performance infrastructure is commercialized for enterprise deployment, the resulting impact spans far beyond standard IT metrics. The core computational engine—combining AMD EPYC™ processors, AMD Instinct™ GPUs, and HPE Cray architectures—delivers the heavy-duty parallel processing required for data-intensive workflows:

  • Tsunami forecasting and climate modeling: Seconds matter when predicting natural disasters. Environmental agencies leverage these co-engineered systems to process massive, multi-variable climate data sets in real time. By accelerating early detection and tsunami simulation workflows, data centers can generate accurate predictive models fast enough to impact emergency response times.
  • Accelerated drug discovery: Pharmaceutical research traditionally relies on years of slow, iterative laboratory testing. By executing complex molecular modeling and chemical simulations on systems built with AMD and HPE, enterprises can screen billions of drug compounds in a fraction of the time. This shifts the bottleneck from raw computing availability to pure scientific innovation.

Right-sized AI: Moving from hype to business

A common misconception among technology executives is that cutting-edge AI requires an unrealistic budget and an army of dedicated data scientists. However, one of the most critical takeaways from AMD and HPE customer case studies is the democratization of machine learning frameworks for small and medium-sized businesses.

Through highly optimized compute nodes like the HPE ProLiant Gen13 portfolio, SMBs can implement pre-configured, turnkey AI environments. These systems run on powerful AMD EPYC™ processors to streamline model training, fine-tuning, and edge inference.

This allows smaller enterprises to optimize supply chain analytics and improve real-time decision-making without having to completely overhaul their existing IT architecture.

The sustainability mandate: Optimizing the modern data center

As processing requirements skyrocket, so do energy demands. Modern CIOs must constantly balance their computational needs with strict corporate sustainability targets and rising utility costs. Resolving this tension requires a holistic approach to server efficiency.

AMD EPYC™ CPUs focus directly on maximizing performance-per-watt. By consolidating heavy workloads onto fewer, more powerful multi-core chips, organizations can substantially reduce their physical server footprint.

When combined with HPE’s advanced thermal management and direct liquid-cooling innovations—such as those featured in the latest HPE ProLiant XD systems—enterprises can drastically slash data center power waste, optimize energy consumption, and systematically lower their carbon footprints.

Security at the foundation

Deploying AI and HPC at scale introduces a massive data footprint, making information security a primary concern for any technology leader. Hardware-level vulnerabilities cannot be patched with software alone.

To address this, HPE and AMD integrate security directly into the physical silicon. AMD’s advanced hardware-based security features complement HPE Silicon Root of Trust and integrated iLO management engines. This creates a highly secure, verified supply chain execution environment where boot codes, firmware, and sensitive AI data models are actively protected against tampering and cyberthreats from the moment the server powers on.

Strategic takeaways for the forward-looking CIO

The evolution of computing has reached a critical inflection point. To stay competitive, IT leaders should evaluate their infrastructure strategy across three core areas highlighted by the HPE and AMD ecosystem:

  1. Prioritize hybrid architecture consolidation: Leverage high-density, multi-core processors to handle virtualization, data analytics, and AI workloads simultaneously on a unified hardware footprint.
  2. Design for energy efficiency first: Transition toward sustainable infrastructure platforms that cut server power draw without sacrificing performance thresholds.
  3. Future-proof for AI scaling: Invest in flexible compute and storage systems that allow seamlessly scaling workloads from edge environments up to private cloud deployments.

Ultimately, the technical innovations outlined in the HPE and AMD Real-World AI and HPC Results eBook demonstrate that exascale-level performance is no longer a distant concept. By deploying infrastructure engineered for maximum power, built-in security, and sustainability, CIOs can transform their data centers into engines of continuous enterprise innovation.

item.title: Beyond the AI hype: Why C-suite control is the ultimate differentiator
item.description:
The initial wave of artificial intelligence experimentation is officially behind us. For C-level executives, the focus has abruptly shifted from “what can AI do?” to “how do we scale it securely without breaking our operational backbone?”

As large enterprises move AI out of isolated pilot programs and into core, enterprise-wide production, a stark reality is setting in: traditional enterprise infrastructure was never built for this type of weight. From deep simulation and advanced analytics to model training, fine-tuning, and real-time inference, the workloads are massively intensive. Every single data asset your organization owns now carries parallel weights—immense strategic value if unlocked correctly, but critical operational risk if governed poorly.

For the CIO, navigating this inflection point requires looking past software applications and focusing heavily on the underlying architecture. The next era of business isn’t just about who has the best algorithm; it is fundamentally about who controls their data, their infrastructure, and their AI life cycle.

Resolving the fragmented infrastructure crisis

The earliest roadblock to successful AI scaling is structural fragmentation. In most sprawling enterprises, data, compute, and operations are scattered wildly across on-premises data centers, colocation facilities, and multiple hybrid clouds. Trying to run high-performance AI workloads across a fragmented environment leads to a catastrophic loss of efficiency, unpredictable latency, and spiraling costs.

To build an AI-ready foundation, forward-thinking organizations are increasingly investing in high-performance computing (HPC) environments specifically engineered to handle data-heavy workloads at scale. By unifying your enterprise data pipelines with integrated AI/HPC systems, you gain the ability to drastically maximize resource utilization.

Through an integrated foundation—like the high-performance platforms powered by AMD EPYC™ CPUs and AMD Instinct™ GPUs—large enterprises can seamlessly cross the bridge between raw storage and real-time computing power. Whether your strategy requires deploying on-prem for maximum speed or leveraging hybrid environments for operational resilience, having a unified structural foundation ensures your infrastructure scales with your innovation, rather than capping it.

Navigating governance and evolving compliance

As your enterprise AI footprints expand, so do the compliance risks. For C-level executives, data privacy, shifting international regulations, and inconsistent internal governance represent multimillion-dollar liabilities. Letting sensitive data flow freely into unverified public models or unmonitored infrastructure isn’t just risky—it’s a direct threat to the business’s longevity.

Operational control requires deployment options that explicitly protect your intellectual property. By maintaining strict control over where critical data lives, organizations can enforce corporate policy and mitigate risk at every stage of the data life cycle. Partnering with technology leaders like HPE and AMD gives enterprises access to secure, compliant, multi-tenant architectures. This tier of security enables your most proprietary data assets to remain locked within trusted environments while still fueling the high-speed insights your business requires to outcompete the market.

Operationalizing at scale with full-stack observability

Moving an AI model from a successful test lab into full-scale enterprise production can be notoriously difficult. Raw performance alone is no longer enough to guarantee value; operational maturity requires comprehensive, top-down visibility across your entire technological ecosystem.

Without an integrated orchestration plane, tracking system health, managing complex workloads, and optimizing daily workflows becomes a guessing game. HPE bridges this operational gap by combining advanced automation, intelligent orchestration, and full-stack observability. This unified control plane gives your infrastructure teams the precise metrics they need to monitor system health, predict capacity constraints, and proactively streamline complex AI and HPC systems. When you can witness exactly how your infrastructure behaves from a single dashboard, you eliminate operational friction and accelerate your time to value.

Trusting the supercomputing pioneers

When scaling infrastructure that dictates the future of your company, relying on unproven architectures is a gamble. Peace of mind comes from working alongside technology partners who have already solved these challenges at the highest levels of computing.

HPE and AMD don’t just talk about high-performance computing—they actively power the world’s fastest and most efficient supercomputers. In fact, HPE delivers six out of the top ten most powerful supercomputers globally and the #1 spot on the HPL-MxP list. By combining HPE’s exascale expertise and advanced data center design capabilities with AMD next-generation processing power, they deliver the definitive, repeatable designs needed to scale enterprise AI with total confidence.

3 Strategic tips for C-level executives accelerating AI

  • Unify first, scale second: Stop launching disconnected AI initiatives across isolated business units. Prioritize the consolidation of fragmented data and hybrid computing infrastructure into a single, cohesive foundation before attempting large-scale deployments.
  • Insist on full-stack observability: Do not accept infrastructure solutions that obscure your view. Demand a unified control plane that provides absolute visibility over system health, utilization metrics, and automated workloads to prevent spiraling operational costs.
  • Keep governance close to the data: Mitigate compliance risks by opting for flexible deployment frameworks that allow sensitive, proprietary data to remain in secure, controlled environments rather than public ecosystems.

item.title: Data sovereignty is reshaping AI infrastructure
item.description:
The cloud-first mandate is hitting a hard, physical reality: the uncompromising need for data sovereignty. As generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) scale across government labs, research universities, and regulated enterprises, organizations are drawing a line in the sand. According to recent Intersect360 Research, the infrastructure debate has officially been settled. Many organizations own their infrastructure, site it locally, and staff it themselves.

The numbers tell an undeniable story of a market moving aggressively on-premises to guarantee data control. Intersect360 Research found that 68.2% of respondents use no public cloud storage at all for active HPC-AI workloads, while 56.3% report zero cloud computing usage for these systems. Crucially, 83.5% agree that data and compute must remain physically proximate, with zero respondents disagreeing. This is not a temporary cost calculation or a transient trend; it is a structural necessity driven by strict regulatory exposure, national security mandates, and the absolute requirements of data residency.

The AI performance penalty

While sovereignty requirements are successfully being met on-premises, a massive new technical challenge has emerged: performance. AI workloads are driving storage architectures toward intense, many-small-file access patterns. Legacy parallel filesystems were originally built for large, sequential data streaming, and they struggle immensely when this access pattern inverts.

The research exposes a widening gap between what sovereign organizations need and what they are actually experiencing:

  • The small-file shortfall: Performance on many small files represents the largest satisfaction gap in the entire study, scoring a massive 0.98 deficit between importance (4.18) and user satisfaction (3.20).
  • The commodity trait ends: A resounding 92.9% of respondents say that storage solutions are strategically important, board-level acquisitions, rather than simple commodity purchases.
  • Absorbing the hit: Buyers are currently choosing to absorb this severe performance penalty rather than compromise on data residency or loosen their sovereignty requirements.

Closing the gap: Sovereign-grade and AI-ready

Organizations should not be forced to trade analytical speed for data ownership. The market is actively demanding on-premises architectures that can deliver world-class AI data throughput and ultra-low latency entirely on the customer’s floor.

This is where the alliance between industry leaders changes the calculus for modern IT leaders. HPE Cray Supercomputing systems, powered by AMD EPYC™ CPUs and AMD Instinct™ GPUs, are proving that sovereign-grade infrastructure and AI-ready performance are no longer competing specifications. This powerful hardware profile is already driving some of the world’s most significant, institutionally owned deployments. These include the Frontier exascale system at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Setonix at Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre, and LUMI at CSC Finland.

By pairing HPE’s deep operational lineage in highly classified, zero-trust environments with AMD’s cutting-edge silicon architecture, enterprises can deploy local clusters designed specifically for the unique metadata and small-file demands of modern AI models.

The new blueprint for data control

Data sovereignty requires satisfying three pillars simultaneously: total ownership of the physical equipment, complete control over data access, and local accountability for security. As regional regulations stiffen across Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East, the transition away from public cloud dependence for core AI assets will only accelerate. CIOs who want to maximize the analytical value of their proprietary data without exposing it to third-party risk must look to partnerships that offer deep regional expertise, flexible financing, and validated hardware architectural depth.

The sovereign AI checklist for CIOs

  • Audit remote access: Verify whether remote hardware vendors maintain administrative access paths that bypass your data sovereignty boundaries.
  • Map data-compute proximity: Identify latency bottlenecks caused by separating active AI training models from underlying data repositories.
  • Benchmark small-file workloads: Test how your current on-premises storage handles AI metadata operations and minor-file access patterns.
  • Assess regional compliance: Review emerging data-residency laws in your operational regions that mandate local personnel and local physical siting.

3 quick tips for CIOs

  1. Don’t compromise residency for speed: The performance gap in small-file storage is a hardware architecture problem, not an indictment of on-premises infrastructure. Look to modern parallel processing systems rather than migrating back to the public cloud.
  2. Vet your vendors’ operational lineage: Look for infrastructure partners with a proven history of operating in highly regulated or classified environments. True security capability is demonstrated through an engineering record, not a product brochure.
  3. Plan for total handoff, not just installation: AI systems require continuous optimization. Contract with vendors that provide comprehensive, step-by-step guidance and long-term local support networks rather than transactional sales.

To learn more about how to design an on-premises infrastructure that balances compliance with performance, read the Intersect360 Research.

item.title: Navigating IT/OT governance: overcoming barriers to achieve proactive compliance
item.description:
Many organizations have formalized their approach to cybersecurity compliance. But having a program in place is different from implementing its requirements consistently across operational environments.

Claroty’s The Global State of Operational Security 2026found that 75% of respondents have a structured or proactive approach to managing cybersecurity compliance requirements for critical infrastructure. Yet 38% cited keeping up with evolving regulations, mandates, and frameworks as a challenge.

Compliance frameworks set expectations but putting them into practice is more complicated. For CIOs and CISOs, that means determining who is responsible for implementation, how to manage risks when conventional controls are not feasible, and how to adapt as requirements and environments change.

Set clear ownership across IT and operations

Information technology (IT) and security teams define policies and controls, while operations teams understand how equipment supports production, facilities or care delivery, and the consequences of changing or taking a system offline. When these responsibilities are split, requirements and implementation can become disconnected, leaving gaps that attackers can exploit.

A security team can set a control without understanding how it affects a particular process. Operations teams may recognize that the control cannot be applied as written, but the lack of authority to approve an exception or decide what risk is acceptable. Without a clear path to a decision, the gap can remain open.

In the survey, 29% identified IT/OT alignment challenges, including gaps in skills, ownership, or collaboration between IT security and operational technology (OT) teams, as the single biggest operational barrier to achieving full compliance across their organization’s cyber-physical systems (CPS).

Leaders need to assign decision rights, not simply ask teams to collaborate. For each requirement, they must determine who interprets it, who implements and verifies the relevant controls, who can approve an exception, and who has the authority to accept the associated risk. Because approving an exception and accepting risk are separate decisions, organizations should establish clear accountability for each and involve the appropriate decisionmakers before an exception is approved. A defined process for resolving conflicts between security requirements and operational needs ensures that constraints lead to a decision rather than an unresolved gap. 

Adapt controls to operational realities

Twenty-six percent of surveyed organizations identified legacy systems that cannot be easily patched or updated as the single biggest operational barrier to achieving full compliance across their organization’s CPS.

A uniform cybersecurity compliance checklist cannot account for the technical limits and business consequences of every operational system. Some equipment relies on older or proprietary technology. Other systems can only be taken offline during narrow maintenance windows. Updating a production controller also carries different consequences from updating a standard IT system, such as an employee’s laptop.

When a system cannot be updated as planned, organizations still need to manage the risk. Prioritization should account for the asset’s role in critical operations, its exposure to threats, and the potential consequences of compromise. Teams should assess vulnerabilities and unmet requirements to determine the most effective response while minimizing disruption to operations. Depending on the risk, that could mean remediation, restricting access, or applying compensating controls. Additional safeguards include segmenting networks to limit the spread of an attack, strengthening authentication, or monitoring unexpected changes.

When remediation is not immediately feasible or a required control cannot be fully implemented, organizations must document how they are managing the remaining risk. Record why the control cannot be applied, what compensating measures are in place, and who is accountable for the risk. Set a review date to reassess whether the exception is still necessary, and that the safeguards remain effective. Apply the same approach to third-party connections, establishing clear requirements for who can access operational systems and what that access allows.

Maintain visibility as environments change

Operational environments and compliance obligations change as organizations add devices, modify configurations, onboard suppliers, and face new or revised requirements. A completed assessment captures conditions at a particular point in time and can quickly become outdated.

CIOs and CISOs should integrate compliance oversight into existing security and operational processes. An accurate inventory of connected assets and the processes they support gives leaders visibility into how systems are exposed, what they connect to, and which controls apply. This visibility helps leaders to identify changes that could affect compliance and focus attention on the gaps that pose the greatest risk to critical operations.

Regular reassessment helps organizations determine whether controls remain effective as assets, configurations, suppliers, and requirements change.

Effective operational compliance requires clear accountability, controls that reflect the realities of operational systems, and ongoing oversight. The goal is to ensure compliance requirements translate into security practices that protect critical operations, not simply to demonstrate compliance during an audit.

item.title: IT leaders seek alternatives for SAP, VMware, and Java
item.description:
CIOs are increasingly looking to shake up their enterprise software portfolios, and no software suite is too large or too entrenched to be off limits for potential replacement.

Driven by increasing licensing costs, end of vendor support, and the promise of AI-coded alternatives, IT leaders are adding several major enterprise software packages to their replacement lists, including VMware, SAP’s ERP suites, and Oracle’s Java. Representatives of those three companies didn’t respond to requests for comment.

One factor driving the trend is the ever-improving functionality of AI-powered coding tools, leading some CIOs to explore building their own software in targeted cases instead of relying on outside vendors.

The potential for AI coding tools to replace SaaS suites drove the so-called SaaSpocalypse, a sharp decline in the stock prices of several SaaS vendors earlier this year. Replacing SaaS products with AI-coded software has largely remained theoretical, at least so far, but a few IT leaders have begun to experiment with the possibility.

At the same time, some software vendors have pushed customers away with more expensive pricing models or the end of support for enterprise mainstays.

Broadcom raised prices significantly after purchasing virtualization market leader VMware nearly three years ago, and a recent survey by third-party support vendor Rimini Street found 90% of IT leaders at VMware customers looking for alternatives.

SAP meanwhile has announced the end of support for its popular, perpetually licensed ECC ERP package and is pushing customers to adopt its subscription-based S/4HANA suite. SAP’s ever-shifting end-of-customer-support deadline has prompted customer backlash.

While VMware and SAP are at the center of the software-replacement bullseye, some CIOs are keeping all options open in hopes of breaking away from ever-increasing software subscription prices.

About 22% of IT leaders are actively reconsidering core enterprise systems such as ERP and CRM, according to research from IT analyst firm Gartner. But many are also actively reassessing niche and point software solutions, especially low-complexity edge applications, says Patrick Connaughton, chief of research at Gartner.

“IT leaders aren’t planning wholesale replacements of core systems yet,” he says, but that’s likely to change in coming years, he adds, with more than nine in 10 IT leaders expecting disruption in the software market. AI agents, for example, are replacing expensive UIs and seat-based pricing, and AI-enabled coding is prompting IT leaders to rethink whether they need to buy enterprise software, he notes.

“Most IT leaders expect their current software models to be upended as customer fatigue with vendor lock-in, bloated suites, and diminishing returns drives a shift away from point solutions,” Connaughton says. “A fundamental buy-versus-build inversion is under way as rapid adoption of agentic coding tools enables organizations to build custom alternatives faster and at lower cost.”

The incumbent advantage

Still, incumbent vendors have advantages, with institutional trust, regulatory moats, and data lock-in keeping most CIOs from making major replacements in the next three to six years, Connaughton says.

Nevertheless, IT leaders see some momentum toward a great software replacement.

John Burns, senior director of finance systems and transformation at equipment rental firm Herc Rentals, eyes ERP as a huge target for replacement, with finance departments often paying twice, once in license fees and again in workarounds. Other finance software tools are also on Burns’ hit list.

SAP ending mainstream maintenance for ECC in 2027 is a significant driver for IT leaders to look for alternatives or for third-party support, Burns says.

“Price increases and end-of-support drive the decision,” he adds. “AI agents aren’t replacing ERP yet. An agent needs a clean general ledger to read from and write to. The ERP underneath stayed.”

Burns has mitigated Herc Rentals’ reliance on its ERP by adding other tools around it. “I surrounded the ERP with best-of-breed tools so they could unplug the ERP on their timeline rather than worry about the product sunsetting,” he explains.

But extricating yourself from a major software vendor is a huge process, Burns admits. Companies need to map data, redesign controls, and retain staff, and before switching vendors, CIOs should ask their CFOs how many business disruptions they’re willing to endure, he advises. If the answer is zero, the CIO may want to reconsider the switch.

“Software companies know the aggravation cost of switching is high, and change is the hardest part,” Burns says. “On every ERP and enterprise performance management migration I’ve run, the license was the smallest line item.”

Kevin M. Coles, founder of factional CIO and CTO firm Coles Technical Group, believes VMware also has a huge target on its back, but other vendors are not immune.

“The licensing change turned a quiet line item into a board-level number,” he says. “Close behind is the long tail of SaaS that’s adding AI tiers and raising prices at renewal, often for features nobody asked for.”

Coles agrees with Burns’ observation that switching can lead to major headaches.

“Customers stay even when they say they’ll leave because the license is rarely the real cost of switching,” he says. “The real costs are the integrations nobody documented, the reports finance depends on, the staff who only know one console, and the year of running two systems side by side. Most surveys measure frustration, not switching cost, so the numbers overstate how many will actually move.”

CIOs should consider how long a switch will really take and the cost of a day of disruption to the business, he recommends. “If nobody can answer, you’re not ready to negotiate, let alone migrate,” he says.

IT leaders should also determine whether the replacement software is actually independent or if it leans on the same identity, cloud, or integration layer they’re trying to reduce their dependence on, he adds.

“The most useful thing a CIO can do is run that exercise now, before the renewal notice arrives,” Cole says. “Even if you stay, a credible exit plan is the best leverage you’ll ever have in the negotiation.”

IT leaders also often talk about replacing their ERP and CRM vendors, but don’t often pull the trigger, Coles adds.

CRM on the list

Pino Soro, chief business transformation officer at low-code app development vendor Quickbase, sees both ERP and CRM systems on the hit list.

“CIOs are taking a harder look at large, expensive platforms where costs keep going up, but flexibility hasn’t kept pace,” he says. “ERP and CRM systems are natural starting points, particularly for organizations that are locked into a vendor or are paying for features their teams barely use.”

Many CIOs are also trying to consolidate their tech stacks, Soro says. “When teams are paying for three or four different tools to manage what could be a single workflow, that’s an obvious place to start questioning the spend,” he adds. “With AI making it easier to build software, CIOs have more options to consolidate, customize, or build their own solutions than they did even a year ago.”

In addition to VMware and SAP, another target for replacement is Oracle’s Java, says Brad LaPorte, strategic advisor at IT advisory firm Lionfish Tech Advisors. All three are on the target list for similar reasons, he adds.

“The vendor changed the deal, not the software,” he says. “VMware changed the price and the packaging. SAP put a clock on ECC. Oracle switched Java to per-employee pricing in 2023, which means a subscriber now pays for staff who’ve never opened a Java app.”

But wanting out and getting out are two very different things, LaPorte stresses. In a survey released in February by cloud management software vendor CloudBolt, 86% of IT decision-makers at large North American companies said they were shrinking their VMware use, he notes. Yet, just 2% of respondents had shifted three-quarters of their environments away from the virtualization giant.

LaPorte compared switching enterprise software vendors to moving between houses.

“Java is a studio apartment — pack a few boxes and you’re out,” he says. “VMware is the house you’ve lived in for 15 years, with wiring from half your business running through the walls, and getting out means opening every one of those walls while keeping the lights on. SAP is the house where the most likely next address is SAP’s newer building, on SAP’s schedule.”

While many companies have looked at alternatives, detangling themselves from a software suite like VMware can take up to four years, LaPorte notes.

“They stay because moving is harder than complaining, and most of the reasons to stay are rational,” he says. “Nobody moves out of a 15-year house in a weekend.”

For IT leaders considering a switch, LaPorte recommends first identifying all their use cases and reasons for the change.

“Inventory before you price,” he says. “Map every workload, every integration, and every admin account that touches the platform, and only then price the exit, because most exit estimates I’ve seen cover the license and miss the wiring entirely.”

IT leaders should also plan for a half-moved house, to extend LaPorte’s comparison to moving between homes.

“For two to four years you’ll run two estates, with two patch cycles, two sets of privileged accounts, and two attack surfaces,” he says. “The old house is the one that gets broken into; because everyone’s attention has moved to the new address, nobody is watching the doors at night, and everybody on the project assumes the locks are somebody else’s job.”

item.title: Culture is the new AI barrier: Why trust and adoption are more than technical challenges
item.description:
There’s intense focus among business leaders on building the right IT foundation to support AI across the organization. There’s a rush to provision computing resources, unify data sources and modernize security, among other investments. But the implementation of AI is both a technical and organizational challenge. To actually get value, employees must know how to effectively wield the tools and understand their role in the emerging agentic processes, both as a security check and a mentor.

Businesses need to trust they have the right infrastructure in place to scale, and employees have to trust the outputs are accurate — particularly as AI agents operate with growing independence. Increasingly, AI can move beyond simply monitoring systems. Agents can start to act like a site reliability engineer, for example, retrying failed jobs, identifying problems and initiating self-healing actions. Or in post-trade processing, AI agents can automate exception management, a traditionally manual process that requires information to move back and forth between financial institutions and counterparties.

To manage both the cultural and technical changes required, companies should think of AI adoption in three layers: foundations, trust and adoption.

Foundations

AI success starts with the fundamentals. At the most basic level, it’s about making sure the resources are there to power the AI agents. But soon enough, any company will be able to buy or rent enough hardware to run AI at scale.

The bigger challenge is actually governing AI activity across the organization. Enterprises need to be able to trace what AI agents are doing, understand the decisions they are making and govern those actions appropriately. And governance must extend beyond access controls and identity management to compliance.

Every industry faces its own regulatory requirements that change depending on the region of operations and use case. For example, financial services firms have to comply with FINRA in the U.S. while medical institutions have to worry about HIPPA and other patient privacy protections.

Organizations need to account for security, reporting, data access and regulatory obligations from the beginning. They need to be able to trace what AI agents are doing, understand why they’re making those decisions and govern those actions appropriately.

The foundation also has to be flexible enough to evolve as AI capabilities change. When governance systems are constructed around a single model, vendor or use case, it becomes a manual, time-consuming process to update or shift. And when organizations move too slowly to adapt, gaps emerge that can cause reputational, financial or operational harm.

As AI agents are increasingly introduced to workflows, it’s a constant balancing act to safeguard what the systems can access, the actions they can take and when a human must intervene. In low-risk processes, for example, AI agents may be able to execute entirely without human intervention. Conversely, a critical function like insurance underwriting must still rely on humans making the final judgement.

Trust

Technology projects fail when organizational change is overlooked. It’s the classic innovator’s dilemma: Companies can build the fastest, most enticing race car in the whole world. But if nobody wants to drive it, the speed gauge never gets above zero.

Today, organizations are stuck trying to navigate a tricky gap. AI is constantly getting more powerful, but employees aren’t equipped to use the technology. Only 19% of leaders believe their workforce is AI-ready, according to KPMG. Those of us who have been around the IT industry have seen capable technology fail not for performance reasons, but because potential users were intimidated, skeptical or scared. 

Machine learning is a great example. When the technology first started to gain traction, many of my fellow security professionals were on guard. The systems operated as a black box, and people had no way to verify the information used to form their insights. Even though the ML models were likely more accurate than humans at identifying vulnerabilities, the trust wasn’t there.

Now, trust threatens to once again be a significant barrier to transformation. For users, trust means proof. In fact, a commanding 97% of executives even admitted to overriding AI decisions because of a lack of transparency into the reasoning behind them, according to a recent industry study. Companies must make sure agents outline their thought process and the actions they take.

Trust also comes down to security. When I first got started in the technology industry, I was doing penetration testing for several small businesses. I’d set up networks and plant honeypots to catch potential intruders. I’d never imagined that, decades later, AI would

operate in a similar way: a system that will stop at nothing to get its reward.

AI is more powerful than any existing defense. If there’s a vulnerability, you can bet AI will find a way to exploit it. Agents will even break out of sandbox environments and infiltrate the open web. This is creating an urgent problem for security leaders. Issues that have been sitting undiscovered for decades are now zero-day vulnerabilities.

The only way to combat AI is to expose and fix the errors before bad actors do. Companies should launch AI attacks on their own IT networks to identify security gaps. And when testing new AI agents, performance should be benchmarked against realistic scenarios. The goal isn’t to eliminate risk, but to understand how AI agents change the equation and put controls around to manage it appropriately.

Adoption

A general-purpose AI model doesn’t inherently know how an organization works — why an engineer would configure something a certain way, the precedence for certain actions or the unwritten rules of the workplace.

In many organizations today, AI is operating like a junior associate. If I were a CISO, I would never put someone at the start of their career alone on the front lines to defend my organization. Similarly, I would never hire dozens of new engineers and let them operate with full autonomy.

AI now provides critical support for teams across the organization. But it still needs the guidance of trained subject matter experts to understand how work actually gets done in the organization. Left on their own, agents are likely to make mistakes. Just analyzing an organizational chart, for example, an AI agent is unlikely to understand who owns decision-making in certain domains. It needs the organizational context that only a seasoned employee can provide.

Similar to how organizations train junior employees, they need a mechanism for domain experts to infuse their knowledge into the AI agent, whether that’s through supplying the right training material or providing continual feedback on the actions or responses. For example, organizations might have to feed their AI models pages of design specifications for the agents to understand the specific requirements of a given job, information like how much power will be required and where sites should be located for maximum impact.

The continuous feedback loop is key: AI produces an output, experienced professionals evaluate it, feedback is captured and that knowledge becomes part of the system’s context for the next task. That is how organizations turn AI from a generic technology into an organizational capability.

Employees need the right training. They need visibility into what AI is doing. They need confidence that the system has access to the right information, that its actions are governed and that there is appropriate human oversight. The AI leaders will be those that treat employees as part of the system. The most powerful models or the largest computing environments don’t matter if companies don’t understand how the workforce and technology must work together.

Foundations provide the technical and regulatory guardrails; trust gives employees the confidence to work with the technology and adoption brings the expertise and feedback needed to make AI increasingly valuable over time. When all three layers work together, AI becomes less of a standalone technology initiative and more of an integrated part of how the organization operates.

item.title: Organizational Politics: The Elephant In The Transformation Room
item.description: Every transformation redistributes power, influence, and opportunity. Treating organizational politics as part of the operating system helps leaders navigate resistance and turn approval into action.

item.title: What kind of management style is needed in the age of AI?
item.description:
As AI increasingly takes over routine tasks and basic information processing, simply using the same AI tools as competitors is no longer enough to differentiate a company. Competitive advantage is increasingly rooted in what makes each organization unique: its philosophy, culture, and accumulated tacit knowledge.

For business leaders, including CIOs, the central question is shifting from “How can AI improve efficiency?” to “How can we foster continuous growth for both our people and our organizations in the AI era?”

Two influential perspectives offer valuable insights into this challenge.

The first is Founder Mode, an essay published in September 2024 by Paul Graham, co-founder of Y Combinator, the influential Silicon Valley startup accelerator. The second is The Founder’s Mentality, a management framework developed by Bain & Company through its extensive research into the drivers of sustained corporate growth and the crises that can undermine it.

Both address a fundamental challenge: as organizations expand, how can they preserve the sense of ownership, entrepreneurial energy, and intuitive decision-making that defined their early success?

In this article, I explore how Founder Mode can serve as a practical leadership approach for sustaining the principles of the Founder’s Mentality—and why this combination may become increasingly important for organizational growth in the AI era.

Founder Mode: Rethinking the conventional wisdom of delegation

As an organization grows, leaders should delegate authority to their subordinates. This is conventional management wisdom, taught in both MBA programs and corporate training courses. Graham challenged this conventional wisdom in an essay inspired by a talk given by Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky.

In his talk, Chesky said that “the conventional wisdom about how to run large companies is mistaken.” After taking the conventional advice to delegate authority, Chesky saw meetings proliferate, bureaucracy take hold, and internal divisions intensify. Employees increasingly prioritized their own objectives over the company’s broader goals, while progress on critical initiatives slowed to a crawl. In response, he undertook a sweeping organizational overhaul: he made every initiative visible, dismantled the divisional structure and reorganized the company by function, and shifted to concentrated decision-making by the senior leadership team. In doing so, he revitalized the company.

From cases like this, Graham identified a style of management distinct from the delegation-centered approach and named it “Founder Mode.” It is the style practiced by Steve Jobs at Apple, in which the top executive makes decisions while staying directly connected to every level of the organization.

One example of Founder Mode in practice is the “skip-level one-on-one,” in which leaders engage directly with employees beyond their immediate reporting line and speak directly with employees two or more levels below them. This gives leaders firsthand insight into day-to-day operations and makes decision-making more transparent. Retreats where the CEO personally leads discussions with the management team are another example.

That said, some critics argue that Founder Mode can easily turn into mere meddling. Graham nonetheless maintains that, even taking that risk into account, it is better to adopt Founder Mode. The distinction between Founder Mode and micromanagement lies in how leaders exercise their involvement. Effective Founder Mode combines a clear strategic vision with direct engagement across organizational levels, while preserving employees’ ability to exercise judgment and take ownership of their work. This ability to communicate a clear vision and strategic rationale is what distinguishes Founder Mode from micromanagement.

The Founder’s Mentality: 3 principles for sustained growth

There is a book that analyzed the themes addressed in Founder Mode before Graham’s essay appeared and distilled them into a prescription: The Founder’s Mentality, published in 2016 by Chris Zook and James Allen of Bain & Company. It is a framework that organizes the traits shared by leaders and organizations that achieve sustained growth into guiding principles, and it rests on the following three pillars.

1. Insurgency

Insurgency is a mindset that drives an organization to challenge industry conventions and established frameworks in pursuit of creating new value. It involves identifying unmet customer needs, questioning traditional ways of doing things, and continuously seeking better solutions. At its core lies a clear sense of mission: “Why do we exist?”

2. Frontline obsession

Frontline obsession is a commitment to placing the highest priority on employees who interact directly with customers and incorporating their insights and feedback into management decisions. It involves creating an environment where frontline employees are empowered to think independently, make decisions, and take action. By accumulating small improvements and learning through continuous experimentation in their daily work, the organization consistently enhances the value it delivers to customers.

3. Owner’s mindset

Owner’s mindset is an attitude of taking personal ownership of the entire company, thinking and acting proactively as a founder would. It emphasizes making effective use of management resources, including time and capital, while prioritizing swift decision-making and execution. It also means cutting through unnecessary procedures and organizational constraints to focus on what truly matters and taking responsibility for delivering results.

Based on these definitions, I have developed my own interpretation of the three pillars and incorporated them into my approach to building organizations.

At the heart of Insurgency is the belief that a company should see itself as a movement rather than merely a business—one that fights on behalf of customers whose needs have long been overlooked. This distinctive sense of identity is precisely what attracts top talent and strengthens employee engagement.

Frontline Obsession means treating the frontline, where employees interact directly with customers, as the most important part of the organization. In 1999, just five years after founding Amazon, Jeff Bezos was already describing the essence of the company as a “customer obsession.” This was long before the concept of customer experience (CX) management became widespread, making his foresight particularly remarkable.

This deep commitment to the business is also reflected in the standards of quality an organization upholds. When founders personally set exceptionally high standards and expect employees to meet those same standards, there is little room for bureaucracy to take hold. Steve Jobs, who insisted that every Apple product meet his exacting standards, is perhaps the clearest example.

When this sense of personal ownership demonstrated by founders spreads throughout the workforce, Owner’s Mindset becomes deeply embedded in the organization, fostering a culture in which people take responsibility and see things through to completion.

According to Bain & Company’s research, companies led by their founders achieve markedly better results than other companies, and the Founder’s Mentality is strongly correlated with performance and competitiveness.

The three pillars are, in effect, the core principles that enable startups to scale rapidly.

Masaya Mori

3 crises that threaten growing companies

Yet as an organization grows, these three pillars weaken. Headcount and departments increase, rules and procedures pile up, and managers become consumed by administrative work. Zook identifies three crises that growing companies face.

  1. Overload. The complexity that comes with scale robs employees of freedom and agility, stifles creativity, and drains the organization of momentum.
  2. Stall-out. Growth slows as operations become more complex and the sense of mission becomes diluted, and this stage arrives suddenly and without warning. A stall-out often leaves leadership teams struggling to understand why growth has slowed and how to regain momentum. There is also a growing sense of urgency as younger, faster competitors gain ground.
  3. Free fall. Growth in the core market comes to a complete halt, and the business model that worked until yesterday no longer works. The leadership team struggles to identify the strategic levers needed to reverse the decline; performance deteriorates rapidly, and the company reaches a point where a turnaround is extremely difficult.

Reviving the Founder’s Mentality to overcome organizational crises

Founder Mode can provide a practical leadership approach to reinforcing the three pillars of the Founder’s Mentality. By staying directly connected to employees and customers, communicating the company’s mission, and empowering individuals to act with ownership, leaders can help sustain an entrepreneurial culture as the organization grows. Founders, and leaders who know the company’s early days, engage directly with employees and instill insurgency, frontline obsession, and an owner’s mindset again and again.

The leadership of Lee Kun-hee, Samsung’s former chairman, is a textbook example.

Even after transforming the company into a maker of high-quality products and raising its profile in global markets, he repeatedly told employees directly, “Our company is now facing the greatest crisis in its history.” This unrelenting sense of crisis, sometimes described as a “perpetual crisis,” was the driving force that sustained the company’s founder’s mentality and led it to become the world’s largest electronics company.

Another key is not to treat Founder Mode as something reserved for founders alone.

Fidji Simo, CEO of the grocery delivery service Instacart, has drawn on her experience at Meta, saying, “At Meta, Mark [Zuckerberg] taught us not only how to be good executives, but how to take big risks and reap big rewards. That is Founder Mode.” When founders share their entrepreneurial spirit with employees and place high value on the challenge of building a business from scratch, they are, in effect, developing the next generation of leaders who will carry the founding spirit forward.

AI may ultimately make Founder Mode more scalable than at any other point in history. As AI takes over information synthesis and routine administrative tasks, it becomes easier for executives to access frontline insights directly, with less time and effort. Executives and the front line can connect directly, without information being filtered or distorted as it moves through layers of management. Technology is making Founder Mode easier to practice than ever before.

Conclusion: Building an organization that continues to evolve

Graham’s essay raises fundamental questions for companies at every stage of growth, whether they are expanding rapidly or struggling to maintain momentum. The Founder’s Mentality provides a framework for understanding these challenges and translating entrepreneurial principles into organizational action.

During my 14 years at Rakuten Group, I witnessed firsthand the company’s rapid expansion. As an R&D leader, I helped navigate a period in which its engineering organization, including global operations, grew twentyfold. That experience reinforced my belief that sustained growth requires constant reinvention and a willingness to challenge complacency—principles that resonate strongly with both Founder Mode and the Founder’s Mentality.

As organizations scale, delegation becomes more widespread, processes grow more complex, and the founding spirit risks fading into little more than a set of formal statements. These challenges can emerge far sooner than leaders anticipate.

How can leaders keep the company’s founding philosophy alive, empower employees to take initiative, and nurture the next generation of leaders? I believe the answer lies in maintaining a direct connection with people across the organization, even as its size and complexity increase.

This approach becomes even more important in the AI era. As AI takes on more routine responsibilities and similar technological capabilities become widely accessible, human judgment and organizational values will play an increasingly important role in differentiation. In this environment, the founding philosophy of an organization can serve as a distinctive source of direction, helping leaders determine which opportunities to pursue, which trade-offs to make, and what kind of value to create.

item.title: Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability with API and Monthly Resets
item.description:
Google Cloud has made spend caps on Cloud Billing Budgets generally available, pausing new usage of a service in a project once a monthly budget is hit, without deleting resources. GA adds an API, estimated live costs, and automatic monthly resets, but caps cover only the Gemini API, the Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions, and overages during enforcement delays are still billed.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
